summary.text: The formal statement quantifies over all natural numbers without imposing \(n\ge 1\), so taking \(n=0\) gives a counterexample: the defining expression has value \(a(0)=0\), although \(0\) is neither \(1\) nor prime.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\Bigl(\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma(n)-2n^2\Bigr)_{\ge 0},
\]
where \(\sigma_2(n)\) is the sum of the squares of the positive divisors selected for \(n\), \(\sigma(n)\) is the sum of those divisors, \(\varphi(n)\) is Euler's totient, and \((x)_{\ge0}=\max(x,0)\) denotes conversion of an integer to a natural number. For positive \(n\), this is the usual expression in the OEIS description whenever that expression is nonnegative.

The proposition being disproved quantifies over every natural number, including \(0\), and asserts in particular that
\[
a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\ \text{or}\ n\text{ is prime}.
\]
We show that this equivalence is false for \(n=0\).

Under the divisor convention used in the definition, the divisor set of \(n\) consists of the divisors lying in the finite interval
\[
\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.
\]
For \(n=0\), this interval is empty. (This convention is necessary because, in the ordinary divisibility relation, every positive integer divides \(0\), so \(0\) would otherwise have infinitely many positive divisors.) Consequently both divisor sums at zero are empty sums:
\[
\sigma(0)=0,
\qquad
\sigma_2(0)=0.
\]
Likewise, the totient is defined by counting integers \(r\) with \(0\le r<n\) that are coprime to \(n\). There are no integers in the range \(0\le r<0\), and hence
\[
\varphi(0)=0.
\]
Finally, \(0^2=0\). Substituting these values into the integer expression gives
\[
\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma(0)-2\cdot0^2
 =0+0\cdot0-0
 =0.
\]
The nonnegative-part operation leaves zero unchanged, so
\[
a(0)=0.
\]
Thus the left-hand side of the asserted equivalence is true at \(n=0\).

Its right-hand side is false. Certainly \(0\ne1\). Also \(0\) is not prime: by definition a prime natural number is at least \(2\) (equivalently, is greater than \(1\) and has no positive divisors other than \(1\) and itself), whereas \(0<2\). Therefore
\[
0=1\ \text{or}\ 0\text{ is prime}
\]
is false.

Equivalently, if the claimed universal equivalence were true, applying its forward implication to \(a(0)=0\) would yield the disjunction
\[
0=1\ \text{or}\ 0\text{ is prime}.
\]
There are two cases. The first, \(0=1\), is immediately impossible. The second is also impossible because zero is not prime. Every possible branch is contradictory. Hence the asserted equivalence fails at \(n=0\), and therefore the conjunction containing it—including the additional characterization of the value \(2\)—cannot hold for all natural numbers. No analysis of the second conjunct is needed once the first conjunct has failed.

This counterexample depends entirely on the domain of the universally quantified proposition: it includes \(0\). The canonical OEIS conjecture is stated only for \(n\ge1\). Since \(0\) is outside that intended range, this argument disproves the unrestricted all-natural-numbers formulation that was accepted, but it does not disprove the original positive-integer conjecture as canonically worded.
